rationale: M60 ontology lane, fsharp pass 2 (2026-10-03) — the second `calls` defect, and the larger of the two. TWO GATES on the label were removed, and each was measured before it was touched. (1) THE CALLEE-LENGTH GATE. `calls` was gated on `fnName.length > 1`, which is not a rule about the program: by the time the branch runs the grammar has already said the callee is a NAME. Instrument B counts 5,313 one-character applications over the 6,619-file corpus in 735 files (2.2% of the label's 246,327 full-extent edges), and the dropped population is BETTER connected than the emitted one — on a 120-file draw of the census's own sample, 32.4% of one-character callees name a symbol the same file publishes, against 22.2% for emitted `calls` in-file (validation/m14/fixtures/fsharp/one-char-calls.ts). `let f x = …` composed into `f 41` is idiomatic F# and the gate dropped every one. (2) THE BARE PIPELINE. The lane's own doc claimed pipe `a |> List.map` reads as a call, and it did only when the pipeline sat in CALLEE position (`f (x |> g)`); the shape F# is actually written in — a `let` whose BODY is the pipeline — was dropped whole. Measured on a 300-file corpus draw: 1,043 bare `|>` infix nodes of which 1,037 carry a NAME on the right, against 580 read in callee position, i.e. the label was missing ~11% of the calls the corpus writes. WHY NO ORACLE CAUGHT EITHER, which is why both are in one fixture: `script/m14/fsharp-truth-oracle.ts` reads `application_expression` and `prefixed_expression` and has no `infix_expression` branch, and its `name.length > 1` test is the analyzer's old gate verbatim. Both sides said nothing and nothing disagreed — the workstream's central failure mode reproduced INSIDE one label. The three forbid rows are the refusals the new rule must make and a naive implementation would break: a COMPOSITION operator (`double >> triple`) builds a function and calls neither, a lambda on the right of a pipe names no callee, and `x = y` is an infix like any other. Trees were read off the wired grammar before the analyzer was run on this file: a bare pipeline is an `infix_expression` carrying an `infix_op` TOKEN and name-node siblings, which is what lets the rule read the operator off the tree and pick the side that carries the callee (`|>` applies the right operand, `<|` the left).

expectRelationships.note: the one-character callee: `f 41` inside `let composed = let f x = … in f 41`. Pre-fix this edge did not exist — the callee is one letter long and the rule refused it. The TARGET is the BINDING SPELLING `<callable>�<binding>`: `f` is a local, this lane publishes no symbol for one, and the separator says so (BINDING_SEP, src/ast/types.ts) while `meta.localBinding` carries the claim the incoming rule verifies. CORRECTED 2026-10-14 (task-99): this row pinned `<callable>#<binding>` while its own note cited BINDING_SEP, which is `�` — the analyzer spelled a literal `#`, so `verifyBindingClaim` found no separator and REFUTED all 24,448 of this lane's local-binding edges (`bindFAIL`, the fleet's only non-zero must-be-zero column). The analyzer now uses BINDING_SEP and this row pins the real spelling.

A CALL — tier usage_contextual: the callee is read from how the source USES the name (an application_expression / pipeline), which is the fleet's tier for call edges. Pinned 2026-10-17 with the #419-D tier pass.

forbidRelationships.note: `let composedOp = double >> triple` on line 28: `>>` is an infix_op token like `|>` is, and it COMPOSES two functions — it calls neither. An edge here would be a fabrication, which is why `>>` `>>>` `>=>` `<<<` are absent from the operator map (measured: 13 bare `>>` in a 300-file corpus draw, excluded on this ground)
the same line, other side: neither operand of a composition is the callee, so neither may appear

`let lambdaPipe x = x |> (fun y -> y + 1)` on line 29: the pipe's right operand is a `fun_expression`, which names no callee. The rule asks for NAME siblings rather than for the last child, which is the difference between reading the pipeline and reading its argument

`let equal x y = x = y` on line 30 is an `infix_expression` with an `infix_op` token `=`. If the rule tested the NODE TYPE instead of the operator it would publish `calls equal -> y` for every comparison in the corpus; the 300-file draw counted 991 bare `=` infix nodes for exactly this reason
ledger R7: no relationship endpoint may be the literal `unknown`
